company_items.summary: AutoZone reported FQ4 EPS of $56.05 vs. the Street's $54.03, but the beat was low quality — 145 basis points of gross margin tailwind came from tariff refunds and another 105 basis points from a non-cash LIFO benefit. Domestic comps missed badly at +1.6% vs. the Street's +3.1%, and the operating expense ratio worsened 100 basis points year-over-year to 33.4% of sales. Management noted improving sales linearity in the final 8 weeks of the quarter and expressed confidence heading into fiscal 2027.

Cognex announced the acquisition of RealSense, the market leader in depth-sensing cameras and vision technology for robotic perception and Physical AI, for approximately $500 million upfront plus an additional $106.5 million. RealSense is expected to generate $80–90 million in revenue, representing more than 50% year-over-year growth. The deal positions Cognex more aggressively in the robotics and Physical AI space.

MillerKnoll posted FQ1 EPS of 53 cents vs. the Street's 36 cents, and notably would have beaten even excluding the 11-cent tariff refund tailwind, with adjusted EPS of 42 cents. Sales missed, declining 3.3% organically to $923.4 million vs. the Street's $943.2 million, though orders rose 3.5% year-over-year. Full-year fiscal 2027 sales guidance was trimmed to $3.88–4.03 billion from $3.93–4.13 billion, while EPS guidance was left unchanged at $1.85–2.15.

Pentair named Bob Hau as its new CFO effective November 1, with current interim CFO Bob Fishman staying on through the transition date. Hau previously served as CFO at Fiserv, TE Connectivity, and Lennox International, bringing substantial large-cap industrial CFO experience to the role.

THOR Industries missed FQ4 EPS at 78 cents vs. the Street's 87 cents, with gross margins falling 230 basis points year-over-year to 12.4% vs. the Street's 13.85% estimate, as management cited stubborn interest rates, elevated fuel costs, and inflationary pressure on household budgets. Revenue came in at $2.311 billion, down 8.4% but slightly above the Street's $2.17 billion estimate. There were some bright spots including healthy dealer inventory levels, structural cost reduction actions underway, and a roughly 75% year-over-year surge in the North American towable RV order backlog, though the company declined to provide formal fiscal 2027 guidance.

Viking Therapeutics shares spiked in pre-market trading after the company reported positive clinical trial results for its GLP-1 drug VK2735, showing 22% weight loss in the trial. The results represent a meaningful data readout for the company's obesity pipeline and drove significant pre-market enthusiasm.

tts_summary:
Good morning. This is a company-specific earnings note for Tuesday, September 22nd, with several names reporting before the open. No broad macro or Fed commentary in this note — let's go straight to the movers.

Starting with AutoZone. The company beat on fiscal fourth quarter earnings per share — fifty-six oh five versus the Street's fifty-four oh three — but the quality of that beat is questionable. About 145 basis points of gross margin help came from tariff refunds, and another 105 basis points came from a non-cash LIFO accounting benefit. Strip those out and the picture gets less flattering. Domestic comps missed badly — up just 1.6% versus the Street's 3.1% expectation — and the operating expense ratio worsened 100 basis points year-over-year. Management did say sales improved in the back half of the quarter and they feel well-positioned for fiscal 2027 growth. Call this one mixed at best.

Cognex is acquiring RealSense — the leader in depth-sensing cameras for robotic perception and Physical AI — for roughly 500 million dollars upfront plus another 106 million. RealSense is expected to put up 80 to 90 million in revenue, growing more than 50% year-over-year. This is a strategic bet on robotics and Physical AI expansion. Bullish for Cognex.

MillerKnoll delivered a genuine earnings beat — 53 cents versus the Street's 36 cents — and even backing out the 11-cent tariff refund tailwind, they still would have beaten at 42 cents. Revenue missed at 923 million versus the Street's 943 million, but orders rose 3.5% year-over-year. Full-year sales guidance was trimmed slightly while EPS guidance was held flat. Mixed, with the earnings quality being a genuine positive.

THOR Industries missed. Fiscal fourth quarter EPS came in at 78 cents versus the Street's 87 cents, with gross margins down 230 basis points year-over-year to 12.4%. Management's tone was cautious — citing interest rates, fuel costs, and inflation squeezing consumers through the key selling season. Revenue was slightly above estimates but the profit story disappointed. The North American towable RV order backlog did surge roughly 75% year-over-year, which is worth watching, and the company is executing structural cost cuts. No formal fiscal 2027 guidance will come until later in the fall. Net bearish.

Viking Therapeutics is the high-energy story this morning. Shares spiked pre-market after the company reported positive trial results for its GLP-1 obesity drug, showing 22% weight loss. That is a strong result and puts Viking squarely in the conversation as a credible obesity pipeline competitor. Clearly bullish.

Finally, Pentair named a new CFO — Bob Hau, effective November first — bringing experience from Fiserv, TE Connectivity, and Lennox. Routine transition, neutral to mildly positive.

Bottom line for today: Viking is the momentum name to watch on the GLP-1 data. AutoZone's beat lacks conviction. THOR is a macro warning sign for the consumer discretionary space. Stay alert.
